label: Sayings I–XXV
paragraphs: I. Are these the only works of providence in us? What words are enough to praise them, or to set them out as they deserve? If we had any sense, what else should we be doing, together and alone, but singing hymns to the divine, and speaking well of it, and going over its gifts? As we dig and plow and eat, should we not sing the hymn to God? "Great is God, who has given us these tools to work the earth with. Great is God, who has given us hands, and a throat, and a stomach, who lets us grow without noticing it and breathe while we sleep." That is what we should sing at every turn; and we should sing the greatest and most divine hymn too: that he has given us the power to understand these things and to use them in the right way. What then? Since most of you have gone blind, should there not be someone to fill this place and sing the hymn to God for everyone? What else can I do, a lame old man, but sing hymns to God? If I were a nightingale, I would do what a nightingale does; if a swan, what a swan does. But I am a rational being: I must sing hymns to God. This is my work. I do it, and I will not leave this post as long as it is given me to hold it; and I call on you to join in the same song.

II. What happens, then? It is as if a man on the way back to his own country came to a fine inn and, because the inn pleased him, stayed there. Man, you have forgotten your purpose. You were not traveling to this place, but through it. "But it is a pleasant place." And how many other inns are pleasant, and how many meadows; but only as places to pass through. Your purpose was the other thing: to get back to your country, to relieve your family of their fear, to do what a citizen does, to marry, to have children, to hold the usual offices. You did not come to pick out the more pleasant places for us, but to live in the place where you were born and where you were enrolled as a citizen.
III. If you find yourself in a crowd, call it the games, a fair, a festival, and try to keep the festival with everyone else.

IV. But I have one whom I must please, one to whom I must submit, one whom I must obey: God, and after him, myself. He has entrusted me to myself and made my will subject to me alone, and he has given me rules for its right use.

V. Rufus used to say, "If you have the leisure to praise me, I am saying nothing." And he spoke in such a way that each of us sitting there thought someone had been telling him tales about us: so surely did he put his finger on what we did, so plainly did he set each man's faults before his eyes.

VI. But what does Zeus say? "Epictetus, if it had been possible, I would have made this poor body of yours and your bit of property free and unimpeded. But as it is, make no mistake: this body is not your own. It is clay, cleverly kneaded. Since I could not do that, we have given you a part of ourselves, this power of impulse to act and not to act, of desire and aversion; in a word, the power to use impressions. If you take care of it, and place in it everything that is yours, you will never be hindered and never impeded. You will not groan, you will not blame, you will not flatter anyone. What then? Do these seem small things to you?" "Far from it." "Are you content with them, then?" "I pray to the gods."
VII. What does Antisthenes say, then? Have you never heard? "It is kingly, Cyrus, to do good and to be spoken ill of."

VIII. "But that would not be like me." That is for you to bring into the question, not for me. You are the one who knows yourself, how much you are worth to yourself and at what price you sell yourself; for different men sell themselves at different prices. That is why, when Florus was considering whether he should go down to Nero's shows and take a part in them himself, Agrippinus told him, "Go down." And when Florus asked, "Then why do you not go down yourself?" he said, "Because I do not even consider it." For the man who has once stooped to consider such questions, and to weigh external things and count up their value, is close to those who have forgotten their own role. What is it you are asking me? "Is death to be preferred, or life?" I say life. "Pain or pleasure?" I say pleasure. "But if I do not take a part in the tragedy, I will lose my head." Go, then, and take your part; but I will not. "Why?" Because you think of yourself as one thread among the others in the tunic. "What then?" Your concern ought to be how to be like other men, just as the thread has no wish to stand out from the other threads. But I want to be the purple, that small and shining part which makes all the rest look fine and beautiful. Why then do you tell me, "Be like the many"? How would I still be the purple?

IX. If a man could take this principle to heart as it deserves, that we are all, first and foremost, born of God, and that God is the father of men and of gods, I think he would never have a mean or lowly thought about himself. If Caesar adopted you, no one could bear your arrogance. And if you know that you are a son of Zeus, will you not be proud? As it is, we are not. Two things were mixed together when we were made: the body, which we share with the animals, and reason and thought, which we share with the gods. Many of us lean toward the first kinship, the unhappy and dead one; only a few toward the one that is divine and blessed. Now every man is bound to deal with each thing according to the opinion he holds of it. So those few, who think they were born for good faith, for self-respect, and for sureness in the use of impressions, have no mean or lowly thoughts about themselves; and the many have the opposite. "For what am I? A miserable little man, and this wretched flesh of mine." Wretched it is; but you have something better than your flesh. Why then have you let that go and fastened yourself to this?
X. You are a little soul carrying around a corpse.

XI. The other day I had an iron lamp beside the gods of my house. I heard a noise at the window and ran down. I found the lamp had been carried off. I reasoned that the man who took it had felt something natural enough. What then? Tomorrow, I said, you will find one made of clay. For a man loses only what he has.

XII. That is why I lost my lamp: the thief was better than I was at staying awake. But he paid this price for a lamp. For a lamp he became a thief; for a lamp he became untrustworthy; for a lamp he became like a wild beast.

XIII. But God has brought man into the world to be a spectator of himself and of his works, and not only a spectator but an interpreter of them. So it is shameful for a man to begin and end where the animals without reason do. He should begin where they do, but end where nature has ended in us; and nature ended in contemplation, and understanding, and a way of life in harmony with nature. See to it, then, that you do not die without having seen these things.

XIV. But you travel to Olympia to see the work of Phidias, and each of you thinks it a misfortune to die without having seen such things. Yet where there is no need even to travel, where you are already there and the works are in front of you, will you not want to look at these and understand them? Will you never see, then, who you are, or what you were born for, or what you have been given the power of sight for? "But some things in life are unpleasant and hard." And are there none at Olympia? Are you not scorched by the heat? Are you not crushed in the crowd? Are you not badly off for a bath? Are you not soaked when it rains? Do you not get your fill of noise and shouting and the other hardships? But I suppose you set all this against the worth of the spectacle, and bear it and put up with it. Come, have you not been given powers to bear whatever happens? Have you not been given greatness of soul? Have you not been given courage? Have you not been given endurance? And if I have greatness of soul, why should I still care about anything that can happen? What will throw me off balance or trouble me, or seem painful to me? Shall I not use the power for the purpose I was given it, instead of grieving and groaning over what happens?

XV. If what the philosophers say about the kinship of God and men is true, what is left for men to do but what Socrates did: never to say, when asked where he is from, "I am an Athenian" or "a Corinthian," but "I am a citizen of the universe"?

XVI. Take the man who has studied the way the universe is governed. He has learned that the greatest, the most sovereign, the most all-embracing community is the one made up of men and God; that from God the seeds have come down, not only to my father and my grandfather, but to everything that is born and grows on the earth, and first of all to rational beings, since they alone are fitted by nature to share in God's company, being bound to him through reason. Why should such a man not call himself a citizen of the universe? Why not a son of God? Why should he fear anything that happens among men? Kinship with Caesar, or with any other of the powerful at Rome, is enough to let men live in safety, above contempt, and afraid of nothing at all. And to have God as our maker and father and guardian: will that not free us from griefs and fears?

XVII. For my part, I think the old man who sits here ought not to be working to keep you from thinking meanly of yourselves, or from reasoning about yourselves in a mean and lowly way. He should be working to keep young men from turning up among you who recognize their kinship with the gods, and see that we have these chains fastened on us, the body and its possessions and everything we need on their account to manage and get through life, and then want to throw them off as burdens, painful and useless, and go home to their kin. That is the contest your teacher and educator ought to be fighting, if he really were one. You would come to me and say, "Epictetus, we can no longer bear being tied to this poor body, feeding it and giving it drink and resting it and cleaning it, and then on its account going along with this man and that. Are these things not indifferent, and nothing to us? And is death not an evil at all? Are we not in some way kin to God, and have we not come from there? Let us go back where we came from. Let us be freed at last from these chains that hang on us and weigh us down. Here there are robbers and thieves and law courts, and the men called tyrants, who think they have some power over us because of this poor body and its possessions. Let us show them that they have power over no one."

XVIII. And then I would say, "Men, wait for God. When he gives the signal and releases you from this service, then go to him. But for now, bear to live in this place where he has posted you. The time of your stay is short, and easy for those who think this way. What tyrant, what thief, what law courts are still frightening to those who count the body and its possessions as nothing? Stay. Do not go without reason."

XIX. Something like that is what ought to pass between a teacher and young men of good natural gifts. But what happens now? The teacher is a corpse, and you are corpses. When you have eaten your fill today, you sit crying about tomorrow and where your food will come from. Slave, if you get it, you will have it; if you do not get it, you will leave. The door is open. Why do you grieve? What room is left for tears? What occasion for flattery? Why should one man envy another? Why should he look up to those who own much, or those placed in power, especially if they are strong and quick to anger? What will they do to us? What they can do, we will pay no attention to; what we care about, they cannot do. Who, then, will still rule a man who thinks this way?

XX. Come then, now that you see these things, look at the powers you have, and when you have looked, say, "Bring on now, Zeus, whatever trial you like; for I have the equipment you gave me, and the means to do myself credit through whatever happens." But no. You sit trembling for fear that some things will happen, and wailing and grieving and groaning over the things that do. And then you blame the gods. For what else can follow from such meanness of spirit but impiety? And yet God has not only given us these powers, by which we can bear whatever happens without being humbled or broken by it; like a good king and a true father he has given them unhindered, uncompelled, unimpeded. He has put them entirely in our power, and has not kept back even for himself any strength to hinder or impede them. You have these things free and your own, and you do not use them. You do not see what you have received, or from whom. You sit grieving and groaning, some of you blind to the giver himself and not even recognizing your benefactor, others led by meanness of spirit into complaints and charges against God. And yet I will show you that you have the means and the equipment for greatness of soul and courage. You show me what means you have for blaming and accusing.
XXI. How did Socrates stand on these matters? How else than as a man should who was convinced that he was kin to the gods?

XXII. For if God had made that part of himself which he broke off and gave to us so that it could be hindered or compelled, by himself or by anyone else, he would no longer be God, and would not be caring for us as he should. If you will it, you are free. If you will it, you will blame no one, you will accuse no one; everything will go according to your mind and God's at once.

XXIII. There are two ways of turning to stone. The understanding can turn to stone, and so can the sense of shame, when a man is set on not assenting to what is plain and on not letting go of what contradicts itself. Most of us fear the deadening of the body and would do anything to avoid falling into such a state; but the deadening of the soul does not trouble us at all. And, by Zeus, where the soul itself is concerned, if a man is in such a state that he can follow nothing and understand nothing, we think that he too is in a bad way. But if a man's sense of shame and his self-respect are deadened, we go so far as to call that strength.

XXIV. If we had applied ourselves to our own work as hard as the old men at Rome apply themselves to what they care about, perhaps we too would be getting somewhere. I know a man older than I am who is now in charge of the grain supply at Rome. When he passed through here on his way back from exile, what things he said to me! He ran down his former life and promised that from now on, once he was back, he would care for nothing but spending the rest of his life in quiet and peace of mind. "For how much of it is left to me?" And I told him, "You will not do it. Once you get a scent of Rome you will forget all this." And if he were given any way into the court, I said, he would push his way in, rejoicing and thanking God. "Epictetus," he said, "if you find me putting one foot inside the court, think what you like of me." Well, what did he do? Before he reached Rome, a letter from Caesar met him. He took it, forgot everything he had said, and has been piling one thing on another ever since. I would like to stand beside him now and remind him of what he said as he passed through, and tell him, "How much better a prophet I am than you!" What then? Am I saying that man is a creature not made for action? Far from it. And yet how is their business like ours? If you look at what they do, you will see. What else do they do all day but count, and confer, and consult about a little grain, a little land, and profits of that sort? Is it the same thing, then, to get a little petition from someone and read, "I beg you to let me export a little grain," and to read, "I beg you to learn from Chrysippus how the universe is governed, and what place the rational creature has in it; and consider too who you are, and what your good and your evil are"?

XXV. A man once asked me to write to Rome for him. Most people thought he had met with misfortune: he had been prominent and rich, and later had lost everything and was living here. I wrote for him in a humble tone. He read the letter, handed it back to me, and said, "I wanted your help, not your pity. Nothing evil has happened to me."

divergences.phrase: τῷ θεῷ καὶ μετ' ἐκεῖνον … ἐμὲ ἐκεῖνος συνέστησεν ἐμαυτῷ
divergences.older: "God, and those who come next to Him" (Crossley, reading τοῖς μετ' ἐκεῖνον with Schweighäuser)
divergences.note: Schenkl prints a gap after "and after him". Two fillings are in use: "those after him" (Schweighäuser, from Simplicius) and "myself" (ἐμοί, Salmasius). Lectio takes "myself", because the next sentence explains it: God has entrusted me to myself. The word is a supplement, not the manuscript.

divergences.older: "I heard a noise at the door" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "I heard a noise at the window"
divergences.note: θυρίς is a window, the same word Epictetus has just used for the window where a man airs his fine clothes and tempts the thief. The lamp stood by the household shrine (παρὰ τοῖς θεοῖς, "beside the gods").

divergences.older: "a citizen of the world" (Crossley, and the usual English)
divergences.note: The word is made from κόσμος, which in this book and in the Lectio Meditations is the universe, the whole ordered system of gods and men that XVI goes on to describe. "World" would shrink it to the earth and its nations, which is the modern sense of "citizen of the world" and not Epictetus's.
